title: Bernstein-Vazirani: n classical queries vs 1 quantum query
problem_statement: Given oracle access to f(x) = s.x mod 2 (inner product over GF(2)) for a hidden n-bit string s, find s.

input.parameter: n = number of input bits of f.
input.size_measure: Query model: cost is the number of oracle calls. The harness materialises the 2^n-entry truth table only so that the oracle can be simulated.

algorithms.name: classical: query the unit vectors
algorithms.idea: f(e_i) is the i-th bit of s.
algorithms.time_complexity: n queries (optimal classically, also for randomized algorithms that succeed with probability > 1/2; PROOFS.md §1, §4)

algorithms.name: Bernstein-Vazirani quantum algorithm
algorithms.idea: Hadamard transform, one phase-oracle query, Hadamard transform. The resulting state is exactly |s>.
algorithms.correctness: H^n sum_x (-1)^(s.x) |x> / sqrt(2^n) = |s>, since sum_x (-1)^(z.x) is 2^n for z = 0 and 0 otherwise (PROOFS.md §3; credit: Bernstein & Vazirani 1997). Deterministic: succeeds with probability 1 in exact arithmetic; in the floating-point simulation the intended outcome has probability 1 - O(1e-15) (PROOFS.md, preamble).

lower_bounds.bound: n queries for every success probability > 1/2, randomized algorithms included
lower_bounds.source: Proved in this entry (PROOFS.md §4): for a uniformly random s, the answers s.x_1, ..., s.x_q to q queries (chosen adaptively) leave s uniform on the solutions of q linear equations over GF(2), an affine subspace of dimension >= n - q, so a deterministic q-query algorithm outputs s with probability at most 2^(q-n). Averaging over its coins, every randomized q-query algorithm also succeeds with probability at most 2^(q-n) on average over s, hence on some s; success > 1/2 on every s therefore needs q >= n. The problem is from Bernstein & Vazirani 1997

relationship: Proven separation in the query model, both sides proved in PROOFS.md: n classical queries (optimal also for randomized algorithms with success probability > 1/2) vs 1 quantum query. It is only a linear (polynomial) gap. Simon's problem gives an exponential one (see simon-classical-vs-quantum); the superpolynomial separation of its recursive version is background, not proved here.

background.statement: A recursive version of this problem gives a superpolynomial separation between quantum and classical query complexity.

verification.method: V1: both algorithms return s, which an independent check confirms against the full truth table, for n = 0, ..., 6, 8, 10 (quantum, simulated exactly with lib/qsim.py) and also 16 (classical). V2 measures QUERY COUNTS reported through lib.qsim.Oracle: classical fits n exactly, and quantum is constant (1 query) for every n. Simulation time is exponential in n and is not the claim. Proofs: PROOFS.md proves every claim of this entry (the exact counts, the correctness of both algorithms and the classical lower bound) and names the deterministic checks of each (tests/test_proofs_query.py, the count-check scripts).

caveats: A separation relative to an oracle. It does not prove that quantum computers are more powerful for any explicit, efficiently computable function, and it does not imply BQP != BPP.
notes: A simple proven quantum query advantage (n classical queries vs 1 quantum query, both proved in PROOFS.md); a recursive version of the problem gives a superpolynomial separation (see background).
